title: At a clothing store
goal: Buy clothes: name colors and sizes, point at items with *questo* and *quello*, and try things on before paying.
bekal: use *questo* and *quello* in the right form
ask for another size, another color, or the fitting room

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Provo la taglia più grande
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a fall jacket. Notice how *questo* and *quello* change form to match the noun.

lines.speaker: Commessa:
lines.id: Good morning, can I help you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sì, cerco una giacca per l'autunno.
lines.id: Yes, I'm looking for a jacket for the fall.
lines.literal: yes, I-look-for a jacket for the autumn.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Non lo so, di solito la media. In Indonesia porto la L.
lines.id: I don't know, usually a medium. In Indonesia I wear an L.
lines.literal: not it I-know, of usual the medium. in Indonesia I-wear the L.

lines.speaker: Commessa:
lines.text: Allora provi questa. È una quarantotto.

notes: **Come mi sta?** = "How does it look on me?" The verb *stare* is used for how clothes fit. The answer is *ti sta bene* (informal) or *Le sta bene* (formal). Asking *è bello?* will be understood, but it asks something else — whether the item is nice, not whether it suits you.

**Italian sizes use numbers, not letters.** Men's clothes 46–56, women's 38–50, shoes 35–46. S, M, L appear in big chain stores, but numbers are more common. They don't line up with US or UK sizes at all.
**Ha ragione** = "you're right", literally "you have reason". Again *avere*, not *essere*. The opposite is *ha torto* (you're wrong). *Sono ragione* isn't Italian at all.
**Ce l'ha?** = "Do you have it?" A short form beyond A1 but heard daily in shops. Learn it as a whole; it pairs with *ce l'ho* (I have it) and *non ce l'ho* (I don't have it).
**Provare means to try**, and trying on clothes is *provare*. The fitting room is *il camerino*. *Posso provare?* is the sentence you'll need most in a clothing store.
**Sconto means discount**, and *i saldi* are the seasonal sales. Sales in Italy are regulated by the state: twice a year, early January and early July, with official dates set by each region.
**Blu never changes form.** A few colors are fixed like this: *blu*, *rosa*, *viola*, *beige*, *arancione* (this one changes only in the plural). *Una giacca blu*, *due giacche blu*.

**Mi piace di più** = "I like it better". The verb *piacere* has a reversed structure that's fully unpacked in the next unit. For now, learn *mi piace* (I like it, one thing) and *mi piacciono* (I like them, several things).

grammars.title: Questo and quello
body: *Questo* (this) behaves like a normal adjective. *Quello* (that) behaves like the article *il/lo/la* — its form depends on the first letter of the next word.
after: Compare with the article table in unit 3: *quel* ↔ *il*, *quello* ↔ *lo*, *quella* ↔ *la*, *quei* ↔ *i*, *quegli* ↔ *gli*, *quelle* ↔ *le*. The pattern is exactly the same, just with *que-* stuck on front.
Before a vowel, *questo* is also often shortened: *quest'anno*, *quest'amica*. This is optional.
Standing alone without a noun, the form is simpler: *Prendo questo.* / *Preferisco quello.*

grammars.title: Colors
body: Some change form, some never do.
after: *Azzurro* and *blu* are both blue: *azzurro* is light blue like the sky and the national team's jersey, *blu* is dark blue. Italian treats them as two separate colors, not two shades of one.

blocks.text: Notice that *i pantaloni*, *gli occhiali*, and *le scarpe* are always plural — just like English "pants" and "glasses". To count them, use *un paio di* (a pair of): *un paio di scarpe*, *un paio di pantaloni*.

blocks.title: Ready-made phrases for the shop
items: *Sto solo guardando, grazie.* — I'm just looking, thanks.
*Posso provare?* — Can I try it on?
*Dov'è il camerino?* — Where's the fitting room?
*Ce l'ha in un'altra taglia?* — Do you have it in another size?
*Ce l'ha in nero?* — Do you have it in black?
*È troppo stretto / largo / corto / lungo.* — It's too tight / loose / short / long.

blocks.text: The first phrase saves you from very attentive Italian shop assistants. Without it, you'll have company for your entire visit.
